candidates.speaker: David Wood
candidates.proposition: First-century Jewish concepts resembling incarnation and two divine powers supply the necessary framework for recognizing Jesus's claims to divine identity.
candidates.attributionBasis: The moderator introduces Wood as the affirmative speaker, and this uninterrupted opening follows his taking the podium.
candidates.loadBearingReason: This establishes the historical-hermeneutical premise on which Wood's subsequent readings of Jesus's words, actions, and reception depend.
candidates.contextSummary: Wood argues that later Christian and Jewish developments obscured ideas once present within Judaism, causing modern readers to overlook claims intelligible to first-century audiences.

candidates.speaker: David Wood
candidates.proposition: Old Testament portrayals of two distinguishable figures acting as Yahweh establish a two-powers framework in which Jesus identifies himself as one divine power.
candidates.attributionBasis: The uninterrupted affirmative opening continues in Wood's voice and develops the two-powers thesis announced immediately beforehand.
candidates.loadBearingReason: This is Wood's principal explanation of how Jesus personally claims divine identity and supplies the conceptual framework for nearly all his textual examples.
candidates.contextSummary: Wood draws on paired Yahweh figures and the angel of the Lord to argue that Jewish scripture distinguished two divine agents, then says Jesus claimed to be one of them.

candidates.speaker: David Wood
candidates.proposition: Jesus's identity should be inferred cumulatively from his words and deeds together with the words, deeds, and reactions of his followers and enemies.
candidates.attributionBasis: Wood explicitly lays out a six-part evidentiary method during his uninterrupted affirmative opening statement.
candidates.loadBearingReason: The proposed cumulative method organizes the ensuing affirmative case and explains why hostile reactions and early Christian practices count as identity evidence.
candidates.contextSummary: After stating the two-powers thesis, Wood proposes examining what Jesus, his friends, and his enemies each say and do as a cumulative indication of Jesus's self-understanding.

candidates.speaker: David Wood
candidates.proposition: Jesus identifies himself as the uniquely divine Son, David's heavenly Lord, and Daniel's cloud-riding Son of Man, thereby claiming to be one of two divine powers.
candidates.attributionBasis: This extended textual argument remains within Wood's uninterrupted affirmative opening and uses his announced category of what Jesus says.
candidates.loadBearingReason: The passages are offered as direct evidence of Jesus's personal claims and therefore address the debate's central question rather than merely later Christian interpretation.
candidates.contextSummary: Wood connects sayings from Matthew and Mark with Psalm 110 and Daniel 7, arguing that Jesus assumes divine prerogatives and the identity of the heavenly Son of Man.

candidates.speaker: David Wood
candidates.proposition: Jesus claims divine status by exercising Yahweh's roles as universal judge and raiser of the dead while requiring honor equal to the Father's.
candidates.attributionBasis: Wood remains the sole speaker and explicitly transitions from what Jesus says to what Jesus does in support of his affirmative case.
candidates.loadBearingReason: The argument supplements titular claims with divine functions and equal honor, making Jesus's conduct and asserted authority independent support for divine identity.
candidates.contextSummary: Wood compares Old Testament descriptions of Yahweh's judgment and resurrection power with Jesus's claims in Matthew 25 and John 5 to perform those same functions.

candidates.speaker: David Wood
candidates.proposition: The earliest Christians treated Jesus as the divine Lord and creative Word, gave him Yahweh's name and honors, and worshiped him as one of the two powers.
candidates.attributionBasis: The material completes Wood's opening before the moderator explicitly announces the end of David Wood's statement and Alex's turn.
candidates.loadBearingReason: Early hymnic, Pauline, and Johannine material is used to corroborate Wood's account of Jesus's identity through the immediate beliefs and practices of his followers.
candidates.contextSummary: Wood invokes Philippians, Isaiah, First Corinthians, and John to argue that early believers applied divine names and honors to Jesus and incorporated him within Jewish monotheism.

candidates.speaker: Alex O'Connor
candidates.proposition: In John 10 Jesus answers the accusation of claiming deity with Psalm 82, identifying his status with non-Yahweh beings called gods and clarifying that he is God's sent Son.
candidates.attributionBasis: The moderator transfers the podium to Alex, whose opening then explicitly addresses David's two-powers interpretation and develops this counterreading.
candidates.loadBearingReason: This directly contests whether a principal Johannine saying constitutes a personal claim to be Yahweh and supplies a delegated-status interpretation from Jesus's own response.

responseIntent.earlierTargetDescription: Wood's claim that Jesus's relationship to the Father places him within the Jewish two-powers framework.

candidates.contextSummary: O'Connor introduces Psalm 82's non-Yahweh gods and argues that Jesus cites it to correct his opponents' inference from unity with the Father to literal divine identity.

candidates.speaker: Alex O'Connor
candidates.proposition: Johannine language about Jesus and the Father being one and mutually indwelling denotes a relationship believers may share, not identity between Jesus and Yahweh.
candidates.attributionBasis: O'Connor continues his opening without a speaker change and repeatedly frames the passages as answers to Wood's interpretation of Jesus's relation to the Father.
candidates.loadBearingReason: The argument targets central proof texts for divine identity and claims that their own parallels extend the same unity and indwelling to ordinary believers.

responseIntent.earlierTargetDescription: Wood's interpretation of Jesus's unity with and relation to the Father as evidence that Jesus is a divine heavenly power.

candidates.contextSummary: O'Connor compares John 10 with John 14 and John 17, emphasizing that disciples are promised the same oneness and mutual indwelling used to describe Jesus and the Father.

candidates.speaker: Alex O'Connor
candidates.proposition: Jesus's 'I am' saying need not reproduce the Greek divine name, and even divine name-bearing can signify delegated authority rather than identity with Yahweh.
candidates.attributionBasis: O'Connor remains the uninterrupted speaker, introduces John 8 as another major christological claim, and carries the argument through the final delivered context row.
candidates.loadBearingReason: This addresses a prominent direct-identity proof text by combining a Greek lexical distinction with a Jewish agency framework in which representatives bear God's name.

responseIntent.earlierTargetDescription: The affirmative contention that Jesus's Johannine sayings and the angel-of-Yahweh tradition identify him personally as Yahweh.

candidates.contextSummary: O'Connor distinguishes the ordinary Greek expression used by Jesus from the Septuagint's divine-name wording, then turns to traditions in which non-Yahweh agents receive God's name and authority.

candidates.speaker: Alex O'Connor
candidates.proposition: John 8:58 can identify Jesus as the eternally planned fulfillment of Abraham’s promised redemption without asserting Jesus’s personal preexistence or identity as Yahweh.

candidates.loadBearingReason: This supplies a direct alternative reading of a principal Johannine proof text and therefore bears centrally on whether Jesus personally claimed divine identity.

candidates.speaker: Alex O'Connor
candidates.proposition: The attempt to stone Jesus does not establish that his opponents correctly understood him as claiming to be God, because misunderstanding and broader accusations of blasphemy are recurring possibilities.

candidates.speaker: Alex O'Connor
candidates.proposition: Jewish name-bearing traditions explain worshipful deference and divine authority without identifying the bearer as Yahweh, while Jesus also presents belief in himself as directed toward the one who sent him.
